deep.reconstruction:
Context. This page belongs to Riemann's essay "Neue mathematische Principien der Naturphilosophie" (dated 1 March 1853). The sheet is not an autograph. It is a later fair copy of Riemann's text, made by a copyist or editor. Evidence: the editorial insertions "((Dazu auf einem Blatt mit Bleistift))" and "[einiges weggeschnitten]", and the dotted ellipses where the copyist did not or could not render the original.

(1) Psychological analogy, no mathematics. Riemann builds on Herbart's psychology. New "Vorstellungsmassen" (masses of ideas) continually enter the soul and quickly vanish from consciousness. Each mental act leaves something permanent, which shows itself later in memory but has no lasting effect on the phenomenal world. So with every act of thought something permanent enters the soul and at that moment disappears from the world of appearances.

(2) Physical hypothesis. By analogy, space is filled with a substance that continually flows into the ponderable atoms and disappears there from the corporeal world. In modern terms each atom is a sink of an aether fluid.

Footnote (+), copied from a pencil slip. Both hypotheses (the psychological and the physical) can be replaced by a single one: in every ponderable atom, matter continually passes from the corporeal world into the mental world (Geisteswelt). The cause of its disappearance is the mental substance just formed there. Ponderable bodies are thus where the mental world acts on the corporeal one. A remark adds that on Herbartian ground substantiality belongs to each individual idea (Vorstellung), not to the soul.

(3) Gravitation via the potential, i.e. Gauss's theorem. The gravitational effect in any region is fully determined by the potential function P of all ponderable masses. Equivalently, P is a function of position such that the ponderable mass enclosed by any closed surface S equals
 M_S = (1/(4*pi)) * ∮_S ∂P/∂p dS.
Modern form: with P = Σ m_i/|x - x_i| we have ΔP = -4πρ. Then (1/4π)∮ ∂P/∂p dS = M_S if p is the inward normal; this is the Gauss/Riemann lecture convention. The copy omits the words linking "Massen" to the integral ("...gleich ... sind").

(4) Fluid model. Assume the space-filling substance is an incompressible, homogeneous fluid without inertia. Assume every atom swallows, in equal times, equal amounts proportional to its mass: sink strength k·m.
- Incompressibility with sinks gives div v = -k ρ. Writing u for the inward flux, u = k M_S.
- The previous page assumed the flow direction is that of the force and its speed proportional to the force. So v = c ∇P, and the flux identity reduces exactly to Gauss's theorem with c = k/4π. [my reconstruction of the implicit link]
- The copy breaks off at "so wird offenbar der Druck ...". The printed Werke text continues roughly: the pressure on the atom is proportional to the flow velocity at the atom's location.

Conclusion stated on the page: the gravitational action on a ponderable atom can be expressed through, and thought of as depending on, the pressure of the space-filling substance in the atom's immediate surroundings. This is an attempt to replace action at a distance by a local, contact-type mechanism.

(5) Final paragraph. The hypothesis necessarily implies that this substance transmits the vibrations perceived as light and heat. This leads into the next page's wave equation y = f(x+αt) + g(x-αt) and its memory-kernel modification.
errors: Sign convention: with P = sum m/r one has div grad P = -4*pi*rho. So (1/4pi)∮ ∂P/∂p dS equals +M only if p is the inward normal, or if P is taken with the opposite sign. The page does not state the convention, though it matches Gauss's and Riemann's usual use of the inward normal.

Not an error by Riemann, but the fluid argument leaves open why the pressure on an atom should be proportional to the local flow speed. For an inviscid, inertia-free fluid the force on a sink is a heuristic claim (the 'offenbar' is unjustified as written). The text breaks off before this is completed.

The copy is incomplete: ellipses after 'Massen' and after 'der Druck', and part of the sheet is cut away at the top. The logical statements of the Gauss law and of the pressure law are therefore truncated.

results.what: Enclosed mass equals (1/4pi) times the flux of grad P through a closed surface
results.modern_name: Gauss's law for gravitation / divergence theorem with Poisson equation

results.what: Gravity explained by an incompressible aether flowing into atoms as sinks with strength proportional to mass; force via local pressure
results.modern_name: Sink (fluid-flow) theory of gravitation, aether-sink model
results.usually_credited_to: Riemann 1853 (published in Werke 1876); related later work by Bjerknes, Karl Pearson (ether squirts, 1891); distinct from Fatio/Le Sage

results.what: Aether also transmits light and heat waves; Herbartian mind-matter hypothesis
results.modern_name: Luminiferous aether unified with gravitational medium
results.usually_credited_to: General 19th-century aether physics; Riemann's version known from the Nachlass

deep.surprise_reason: This passage of 'Neue mathematische Principien der Naturphilosophie' was printed by Dedekind and Weber in Riemann's Gesammelte Werke (1876). Historians know it well, including the aether-sink theory of gravity and the Herbartian psychology. The mathematics on the page is the standard Gauss flux theorem.

checkable.asserts: The potential 1/r of a point mass is harmonic away from the mass (result 0).
Outward flux of grad(1/r) through a sphere is -4*pi. Hence (1/4pi)∮ dP/dp dS = m with p the inward normal.
The velocity field of a point sink, v = (k/4pi) grad(m/r), is divergence-free (incompressible) outside the atom.
The inflow through any sphere around the atom equals k*m, i.e. it is proportional to the atom's mass, as the hypothesis requires.

transcription_corrections: The handwriting is a copyist's fair copy, not Riemann's autograph. The ellipses ('Massen . . .', 'der Druck . . .') are in the manuscript itself, marking gaps in the copied source.
The pencil note at the top, '[einiges weggeschnitten]', is plausible but uncertain; it is written in brackets in pencil above the text.

The last pencil line, read as 'Zeyss[?] Mem.[?] ++) S. 23', is very uncertain. A struck-through '++)' precedes it, and it appears to be a cross-reference to page 23 (perhaps 'Zusatz' or a similar word rather than 'Zeyss').
